claim: Twin CMG complexes are assembled head-to-head around duplex DNA at eukaryotic origins of replication.
source: Twin CMG complexes are assembled head-to-head around duplex DNA at eukaryotic origins of replication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction regarding CMG assembly at origins.

claim: Mcm10 activates CMGs to form helicases that encircle single-strand (ss) DNA and initiate bidirectional forks.
source: Mcm10 activates CMGs to form helicases that encircle single-strand (ss) DNA and initiate bidirectional forks.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations in the introduction (Douglas et al., 2018; Heller et al., 2011; Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).

claim: S. cerevisiae CMG tracks with force while encircling double-stranded (ds) DNA.
source: Here we show that S. cerevisiae CMG tracks with force while encircling double-stranded (ds) DNA
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2 using T-substrates that require force to melt non-homologous arms.

claim: In the presence of Mcm10, CMG melts long blocks of dsDNA while it encircles dsDNA.
source: in the presence of Mcm10 the CMG melts long blocks of dsDNA while it encircles dsDNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figures 2 and 4, showing CMG+Mcm10 can melt up to 60 bp (Figure 2) and 150 bp (Figure 4) of dsDNA.

claim: CMG tracks mainly on the 3'−5' strand during duplex translocation.
source: We demonstrate that CMG tracks mainly on the 3'−5' strand during duplex translocation
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3 using methylphosphonate linkages on either strand, showing reduced unwinding when methylphosphonates are on the 3'-5' strand.

claim: Head-to-head CMGs at an origin exert force on opposite strands.
source: predicting that head-to-head CMGs at an origin exert force on opposite strands.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that CMG tracks mainly on the 3'-5' strand and the head-to-head orientation of CMGs at origins.

claim: CMGs that encircle double strand DNA in a head-to-head orientation melt the duplex in an Mcm10-dependent reaction.
source: we show that CMGs that encircle double strand DNA in a head-to-head orientation melt the duplex in an Mcm10-dependent reaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4 using a two-tailed substrate that allows loading of head-to-head CMGs.

claim: Cellular replicative DNA helicases are hexameric ring-shaped motors that track on single-strand (ss) DNA, acting as a wedge to unwind the duplex.
source: Cellular replicative DNA helicases are hexameric ring-shaped motors that track on single-strand (ss) DNA, acting as a wedge to unwind the duplex (Lyubimov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lyubimov et al., 2011.

claim: In bacteria, the circular helicase is a homohexamer that directly assembles onto an AT-rich ssDNA region melted by initiator proteins.
source: In bacteria, the circular helicase is a homohexamer that directly assembles onto an AT-rich ssDNA region melted by initiator proteins
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial replication initiation.

claim: In eukaryotes, the origin recognition complex (ORC) does not unwind DNA.
source: but in eukaryotes the origin recognition complex (ORC) does not unwind DNA (Bleichert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bleichert et al., 2017.

claim: In G1-phase, two Mcm2-7 hexamer rings are assembled head-to-head (N-to-N) around double-strand (ds) DNA by ORC, Cdt1 and Cdc6.
source: Instead, in G1-phase, two Mcm2-7 hexamer rings are assembled head-to-head (N-to-N) around double-strand (ds) DNA by ORC, Cdt1 and Cdc6 (Bell and Labib, 2016; Evrin et al., 2009; O'Donnell et al., 2013; Remus et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Bell and Labib, 2016; Evrin et al., 2009; O'Donnell et al., 2013; Remus et al., 2009).

claim: In S-phase, additional factors assemble Cdc45 and GINS onto each Mcm2-7 to form two replicative helicases on dsDNA oriented head-to-head.
source: In S-phase, additional factors assemble Cdc45 and GINS onto each Mcm2-7 to form two replicative helicases on dsDNA oriented head-to-head (Ilves et al., 2010; Moyer et al., 2006; Parker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Ilves et al., 2010; Moyer et al., 2006; Parker et al., 2017).

claim: Each CMG helicase contains 11 different subunits.
source: Each helicase contains 11 different subunits
evidence: This is stated as a fact about CMG composition.

claim: The term CMG was coined because it contains Cdc45, Mcm2-7, and the four subunit GINS complex.
source: the term CMG (Cdc45, Mcm2-7, GINS) was coined because it contains Cdc45, Mcm2-7, and the four subunit GINS complex (Ilves et al., 2010; Moyer et al., 2006; Parker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ilves et al., 2010; Moyer et al., 2006; Parker et al., 2017).

claim: Mcm10 is required to activate each CMG to encircle ssDNA for bidirectional replication.
source: Mcm10 is required to activate each CMG to encircle ssDNA for bidirectional replication (Douglas et al., 2018; Heller et al., 2011; Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Douglas et al., 2018; Heller et al., 2011; Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).

claim: Recent electron microscopy (EM) studies of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S.c.) CMG at a replication fork show that CMG tracks on ssDNA with its N-tier facing the fork.
source: Recent electron microscopy (EM) studies of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S.c.) CMG at a replication fork show that CMG tracks on ssDNA with its N-tier facing the fork (Douglas et al., 2018; Georgescu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to EM studies (Douglas et al., 2018; Georgescu et al., 2017).

claim: N-first movement of CMG implies that head-to-head CMGs at the origin are directed toward one another when assembled around duplex DNA.
source: N-first movement of CMG implies that head-to-head CMGs at the origin are directed toward one another when assembled around duplex DNA.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the N-first movement observation.

claim: Each CMG blocks the forward movement of the other when oriented head-to-head at origins.
source: Thus, each CMG blocks the forward movement of the other

claim: The duplex must be unwound a sufficient distance for both CMGs to expel one strand for their transition from dsDNA to ssDNA.
source: and the duplex must be unwound a sufficient distance for both CMGs to expel one strand for their transition from dsDNA to ssDNA, which they must do to pass one another and form bidirectional forks

claim: The last steps of origin initiation require the Mcm10 protein.
source: These last steps of origin initiation require the Mcm10 protein (Douglas et al., 2018; Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Douglas et al., 2018; Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).

claim: Mcm10 contains a DNA binding region.
source: Mcm10 contains a DNA binding region (Warren et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Warren et al., 2008.

source: and interaction with the N-terminal regions of Mcm2 and Mcm6 has been demonstrated (Douglas and Diffley, 2016; Lõoke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Douglas and Diffley, 2016; Lõoke et al., 2017).

claim: Cross-linking/mass spectrometry studies reveal a large surface area of CMG-Mcm10 interaction that includes 6 of the 11 CMG subunits.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Mayle et al., 2019.

claim: Recent studies demonstrate a disruption of tight connections between the Mcm2-7 hexamers upon maturation to CMGs.
source: Recent studies of CMG formation at origins demonstrate a disruption of tight connections between the Mcm2-7 hexamers upon maturation to CMGs and untwisting of ~0.7 turns of the double helix per CMG (Douglas et al., 2018).

claim: CMG formation at origins results in untwisting of ~0.7 turns of the double helix per CMG.
source: Recent studies of CMG formation at origins demonstrate a disruption of tight connections between the Mcm2-7 hexamers upon maturation to CMGs and untwisting of ~0.7 turns of the double helix per CMG (Douglas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Douglas et al., 2018.

claim: The observed untwisting of 0.7 turns per CMG is too little for CMG to transition to ssDNA.
source: However, even if the observed untwisting was due to actual DNA melting, it is too little for CMG to transition to ssDNA (Douglas et al., 2018).

claim: CMG and Mcm10 together produce sufficient force to open several turns of the duplex while encircling dsDNA.
source: In this report we use recombinant CMG and Mcm10 and find that, together, they produce sufficient force to open several turns of the duplex while encircling dsDNA

claim: Initial unwinding of DNA by CMG-Mcm10 can occur without the participation of other replication initiation factors.
source: Hence, initial unwinding of DNA by CMG-Mcm10 can occur without the participation of other replication initiation factors.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4 using only recombinant CMG and Mcm10.

claim: CMG has only weak activity in melting 20 bp arms and cannot destabilize 30 bp or 60 bp arms without Mcm10.
source: CMG has only weak activity in melting the 20 bp arms and cannot destabilize the 30 bp or 60 bp arms (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Upon adding Mcm10, CMG unwound all three T-substrates (T20, T30, and T60).
source: However, upon adding Mcm10, CMG unwound all three T-substrates (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Mcm10 alone has no activity in T-substrate unwinding assays.
source: Mcm10 alone has no activity in these assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mcm10 stimulates CMG helicase activity.
source: The results are consistent with prior studies showing Mcm10 stimulates CMG helicase activity
evidence: This is consistent with prior studies and supported by the current experimental data.

claim: Mcm10 enhances CMG processivity during unwinding.
source: enhances CMG processivity during unwinding (Langston et al., 2017; Lõoke et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Langston et al., 2017; Lõoke et al., 2017).

claim: The extent of unwinding decreases as the length of the non-homologous arms increases.
source: The extent of unwinding decreases as the length of the non-homologous arms increases
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data from Figure 2.

claim: The phi29 DNA packaging motor tracks on only one strand while encircling dsDNA.
source: Two of the most well-studied examples are the phi29 DNA packaging motor, which tracks on only one strand while encircling dsDNA (Aathavan et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aathavan et al., 2009.

claim: The bacterial clamp loader surrounds dsDNA but contacts only one strand.
source: and the bacterial clamp loader that also surrounds dsDNA but contacts only one strand (Simonetta et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simonetta et al., 2009.

claim: The cryoEM structure of CMG on forked DNA shows that the translocation strand adopts a B-form spiral shape in the motor domains.

evidence: This is supported by citations to cryoEM structures (Abid Ali et al., 2016; Georgescu et al., 2017) and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A spiral of ssDNA in the central channel is a common feature of all replicative helicase structures examined thus far.
source: A corresponding spiral of ssDNA in the central channel is a common feature of all replicative helicase structures examined thus far (Gao et al., 2019; O'Donnell and Li, 2018; Parker et al., 2017).

claim: When methylphosphonate linkages were on the 3'−5' strand, duplex unwinding was significantly reduced compared to methylphosphonate linkages on the opposite strand.
source: When the methylphosphonate linkages were on the 3'−5' strand in the direction of unwinding, duplex unwinding was significantly reduced compared to methylphosphonate linkages on the opposite strand (Figure 3B,C).

claim: In the inactive Mcm2-7 double hexamer, each ring makes an equal number of contacts with the 3'−5' and 5'−3' strands.
source: This is noteworthy given that in the inactive Mcm2-7 double hexamer, each ring makes an equal number of contacts with the 3'−5' and 5'−3' strands (Abid Ali et al., 2017; Noguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Abid Ali et al., 2017; Noguchi et al., 2017).

claim: Duplex DNA interaction by the MCM and by the CMG is fundamentally different.
source: Hence, duplex DNA interaction by the MCM and by the CMG is fundamentally different.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in strand contacts between inactive Mcm2-7 and active CMG.

claim: CMG readily unwinds the two-tailed substrate in the presence of Mcm10.
source: As shown in Figure 4B (lanes 1–5), CMG readily unwinds the two-tailed substrate in the presence of Mcm10.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4B, lanes 1-5.

claim: Unwinding of the two-tailed substrate continues well beyond the time of addition of the trap oligo.
source: Moreover, unwinding continues well beyond the time of addition of the trap, thereby excluding the possibility that additional CMG loading events are required for unwinding (see Figure 4B and C; also see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for effectiveness of the trap).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The unwinding reaction is absolutely dependent on addition of Mcm10.
source: The reaction is absolutely dependent on addition of Mcm10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The unwinding reaction requires ATP and CMG.
source: and also requires ATP and CMG (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

source: showing that the observed unwinding is the product of CMG's ATP-dependent motor activity coupled to Mcm10 function rather than the product of either CMG or Mcm10 acting separately.

claim: The reaction requires loading of head-to-head CMG complexes because duplexes with only a single CMG loading tail at one end or the other were essentially inactive compared to the two-tailed substrate.
source: The reaction also requires loading of head-to-head CMG complexes because duplexes with only a single CMG loading tail at one end or the other were essentially inactive compared to the two-tailed substrate (Figure 4B, lanes 6–15 and Figure 4C).

claim: Head-to-head CMG complexes, along with Mcm10, can perform the DNA melting required at origins of replication without the participation of any other factors.
source: In overview, these results demonstrate that head-to-head CMG complexes, along with Mcm10, can perform the DNA melting required at origins of replication without the participation of any other factors.

claim: The results are consistent with the action of two independent CMGs colliding with one another on dsDNA, in contrast to the highly interconnected and interdependent but inactive Mcm2-7 complexes within the double hexamer.
source: Furthermore, the results are consistent with the action of two independent CMGs colliding with one another on dsDNA, in contrast to the highly interconnected and interdependent but inactive Mcm2-7 complexes within the double hexamer.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing independent CMG loading and activity.

claim: The product expected for CMG encircling dsDNA and melting both arms simultaneously was ~10% of total substrate.
source: In contrast, the product expected for CMG encircling dsDNA and melting both arms simultaneously was ~10% of total substrate (*AB in Figure 5B,C), as observed in Figure 2 for the 60 bp arm substrate.

claim: Continuous ssDNA translocation during the entire experiment was a minor outcome (~5%).
source: Continuous ssDNA translocation during the entire experiment was a minor outcome (~5%, *A in Figure 5B,C)

claim: A ssDNA gate was previously demonstrated for Drosophila CMG.
source: While we cannot distinguish between these two mechanisms, we note that an ssDNA gate was previously demonstrated for Drosophila CMG (Ilves et al., 2010; Moyer et al., 2006)

source: and subsequently shown to generalize to human CMG and S. cerevisiae CMG (Kang et al., 2012; Langston and O'Donnell, 2017).

evidence: This is supported by citation to Wasserman et al., 2018.

source: The results presented in this report demonstrate that CMG + Mcm10 translocates on dsDNA with sufficient force to melt at least 60 bp (Figure 2)

claim: Head-to-head CMGs can melt up to 150 bp.
source: and that head-to-head CMGs can melt up to 150 bp (Figure 4).

source: The head-to-head CMGs can be added individually and thus are uncoupled and do not need to be intimately connected as in the Mcm2-7 double hexamer.

source: DNA melting by head-to-head CMGs directed against one another is expected to require a force of 65 pN, the force demonstrated to melt dsDNA in single-molecule experiments with optical traps attached to the ends of opposite strands of a linear duplex (King et al., 2016; van Mameren et al., 2009).

claim: Generation of 50–60 pN force has precedent in phage packaging motors.

source: In the case of origin melting, two CMG + Mcm10 are utilized and thus each CMG would only need half the 65 pN required for the ds-to-ssDNA phase transition.

source: While bacterial origin binding proteins melt enough DNA for two hexameric helicases to assemble directly onto ssDNA
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial replication initiation.

claim: Each CMG is demonstrated to untwist about 0.7 turns apiece.
source: Each CMG is demonstrated to untwist about 0.7 turns apiece (Douglas et al., 2018)

source: Indeed, recent studies show that the two CMGs at an origin can drift apart in buffer lacking ATP, indicating they are no longer tightly attached as in the Mcm2-7 double hexamer and are capable of backward slippage (Douglas et al., 2018).
